newsitem.title: UK: Calmer sterling off highs in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: Calmer sterling off highs in late Europe.

text.p: Sterling's fall from four-year highs against the German mark on Tuesday was the first major dent in a four-month bull market but analysts do not think the pound has reached the end of the road yet.

The currency's rise to its highest level against the mark since Britain's exit from the European exchange rate mechanism in September 1992 is soundly based, say economists, even if its rally on the dollar seems to have run its course for now.

Concern about the impact on UK exporters of the pound's 12 percent rise against a trade-weighted basket of currencies since August may act as a drag on the pound but concerted government or central bank action to cap it is unlikely.
The fundamental economic reasons for sterling's revaluation this year have not changed and exporter concerns were not the trigger for yesterday's reversal, according to some analysts.

"The severe whipsaw yesterday means it's hard to get a grip on exactly what's going on short-term, but fundamentally the story is still the same," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at Union Bank of Switzerland in London.
"Sterling will trade in a higher range next year, and where we are now is probably the lower end of it."
Britain's economic growth will again outstrip core Europe next year, leaving short-term UK interest rates nearly twice Franco-German levels and rising.

Growing pressure within Europe to push for a higher dollar against a post-1999 single European currency, which sterling is unlikely to participate in initially, is expected to be an added fillip for the pound.
At 1404 GMT, the pound was trading at 2.5570 marks, eight pfennigs down from a high Tuesday of 2.6370. Against the dollar, it was at $1.6351 compared with $1.6810 early Tuesday.

While Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke on Tuesday acknowledged the curb on exporter competitiveness of a higher pound, he said this is simply a consequence of the floating exchange rate policy in place since the ERM exit in 1992.

Industry protests at the rising pound have grown more vocal in recent weeks. "Many companies have very carefully and pragmatically built up their export positions over the last two to three years and they are now beginning to feel the pinch," said David Botterill, chief executive of the Engineering Employers' Federation in the West Midlands.

Yet traders dismissed talk that the Bank of England was actively intervening to influence the pound on Tuesday and said the central bank was most likely both buying and selling the pound to smooth out skewed trading moves.

The speed and extent of sterling's rise this week may have prompted the central bank to calm the market by selling pounds at the highs but it was likely to have been doing the opposite as sterling tumbled later in the day, they said.
What more likely happened on Tuesday was that a surge in demand for dollars against European currencies in general reinforced a firm cap on the sterling/dollar rate at $1.6900.

This frustrated international fund managers who, according to one recent survey by U.S. investment house Merrill Lynch, amassed their highest portfolio weightings of sterling in almost eight years during the three months to November.

The temptation to take profits on these positions, as the year comes to a close, unleashed a wave of sterling sales against the dollar. The spillover weakened the pound against the mark, with a string of automatic sell orders placed along the steep run higher then triggered on the way down.

"It is clear that sentiment must take a severe knock after such a sharp decline yesterday but the longer-term underlying support for sterling remains intact, regardless of the choppy year-end trading likely in the weeks ahead," said Adrian Schmidt, economist at Chase Investment Bank.
